claims.text: High-temperature stability of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles is governed jointly by high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion.
The proposed stabilization remains effective when noble metals are present only at low levels.
The initial nanoparticles are well-mixed, random, near-equiatomic solid solutions.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes produce severe lattice distortion in HEAs.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a disordered solid-solution phase over intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
Severe lattice distortion increases atomic-diffusion energy barriers and lowers atomic diffusivity.
Reduced diffusivity and entropy stabilization jointly slow or prevent phase segregation at elevated temperature.
Reduced diffusivity and entropy stabilization prevent nanoparticle coarsening at elevated temperature.
Systematic changes in compositional ratios can modulate atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch also maximizes configurational entropy.
High-mismatch nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than lower-mismatch nanoparticles under identical thermal conditions.
High-mismatch nanoparticles will exhibit less structural coarsening than lower-mismatch nanoparticles.
High-mismatch nanoparticles will better retain surface catalytic features and catalytic activity.
The ranges 773–1173 K and 473–1923 K are service-relevant for catalytic and thermoelectric applications, respectively.
Using an inert or controlled atmosphere minimizes extrinsic oxidation effects during thermal exposure.
Initially phase-segregated nanoparticles or systems dominated by oxidation may follow stability mechanisms different from the proposed entropy–distortion mechanism.
Surface-energy effects and minor oxidation can influence quantitative distortion thresholds and temperature limits.
